answer: A tourist attraction that genuinely impressed me was the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, which stretches across the south-west of Bangladesh and into India. I visited it about two years ago on a three-day boat tour that started from Khulna. It is a vast, [[remote]] wilderness, famous for being home to the Royal Bengal Tiger. Gliding through the narrow waterways surrounded by dense forest was an unforgettable experience. The mangrove trees themselves were fascinating, with their roots sticking up out of the mud like hundreds of little spikes, which helps them breathe when the tide comes in. We slept on the boat, and at night the silence was broken only by the calls of birds and the sound of the water. What made it so special was how [[untamed]] everything felt; this was nature completely on its own terms. During the day we took smaller boats into the creeks and walked along wooden trails with armed forest guards. We spotted deer, monkeys, exotic birds and even crocodiles, though sadly no tigers. The whole trip was genuinely [[exhilarating]], partly because of the slight sense of danger. Our guide explained how ecologically important the area is, especially as a natural barrier that protects the coast from cyclones, which deepened my appreciation. I found the sheer scale and [[biodiversity]] of the place utterly [[captivating]]. Honestly, it is one of the few tourist attractions that fully [[lived up to the hype]]. It also made me realise how vital it is to protect such fragile natural wonders before they disappear, especially as rising sea levels are already putting the forest under pressure.

followUps.q: Would you go back to the Sundarbans?
followUps.answer: Yes, I would love to, ideally in a different season to see how it changes. And of course I am still hoping that one day I will be lucky enough to catch a glimpse of a tiger.

followUps.q: Is it popular with foreign tourists?
followUps.answer: It attracts some foreign visitors, but I think it is still underrated internationally. Most tourists there are Bangladeshis, which is a pity, because it is genuinely one of the most remarkable places in the region.
